title: Nucleus Labs - POC scoping: latency & throughput SLOs
summary: POC scoping for latency and throughput SLOs. Discussed TTFT vs TPOT definitions, target p95/p99 numbers, workload sizing (RPS, concurrency, token lengths), benchmarking plan (synthetic vs production replay), success criteria for pilot, and a 2-week timeline to run benchmarks and iterate on config (batching, quantization, KV caching).
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, we're excited to scope the POC for latency SLOs, we'll focus on TTFT and TPOT targets and how to measure them.
[00:12] Dr. Sara Gomez: thanks, yeah latency is the blocker for user experience, worst are the first token times when chat starts.
[00:22] Liam Chen: quick intro from me, Liam (Redwood SE) — I'll run the benchmark plan with you; I'm going to ask about traffic shape, payload sizes, and success criteria.
[00:34] Aaron Lee: our target is to make interactions feel instant — we're aiming for sub-200ms for first meaningful token ideally, p95. p99 can be higher but not worse than 400ms.
[00:45] Priya Nair: product wants 95th < 150ms for TTFT for logged-in customers on our main flow, but we can relax for lower tiers.
[00:55] Maya Patel: okay good, let's align on terminology — we use TTFT (time-to-first-token) for the latency until the first token is emitted, and TPOT (time-per-output-token or time-per-token) for steady-state per-token generation. Sometimes our docs call TTFT TTFB, so you might see both.
[01:12] Dr. Sara Gomez: that mismatch in terms is why we had confusions, got it.
[01:18] Liam Chen: practical targets we typically see: TTFT p95 around 50-250ms depending on model and config; TPOT median 6-15ms for medium models on recent GPUs. For planning the POC we should decide on concrete numbers.
[01:33] Aaron Lee: ok concrete — for the POC baseline can we aim for: TTFT p95 <= 150ms, TTFT p99 <= 300ms, TPOT p95 <= 15ms, TPOT p99 <= 30ms?
[01:46] Maya Patel: yes that's reasonable for a Dedicated-like env with KV cache warmed and batch size 1. We'll note where warm vs cold cache matters.
[01:55] Priya Nair: question — our typical prompt length is 1200 tokens average, response about 150 tokens; but we have longer docs where it goes to 2-3k tokens. How does that affect TPOT?
[02:10] Liam Chen: TPOT is mostly dependent on model compute and hardware; longer outputs increase total time linearly, but per-token times should be similar. However attention compute and KV cache behavior on long context can raise TTFT slightly because of KV merge. We'll include two workloads: short (150 tokens output) and long (1500 tokens output).
[02:28] Dr. Sara Gomez: our traffic shape: peak 200 rps for the small cohort feature, realistic steady around 40 rps, concurrency around 60 workers in frontend. We'll provide production traces.
[02:40] Maya Patel: perfect — for workload sizing we'll run benchmarks at these points: steady 40 rps, burst 200 rps, and concurrency sweep 1-100. Also include warm vs cold KV cache tests.
[02:54] Aaron Lee: what about batching? We prefer latency over token cost, so batch size 1 is default; but we can explore small batching if cost savings are big.
[03:05] Liam Chen: we'll test batch size 1 and 4, and quantized vs FP16 variants. Note quantization can increase TPOT slightly but reduce cost. We'll capture throughput/latency tradeoffs.
[03:18] Priya Nair: measurement plan? we need reproducible scripts and metrics.
[03:21] Liam Chen: plan: 1) replay a sample of production traffic (we'll take a 1k request sample with distribution of prompt lengths); 2) synthetic ramp tests: steady-state 40 rps for 10 minutes, burst 200 rps for 5 minutes; 3) cold starts: restart model pool and measure TTFT cold vs warm; 4) per-token profiling: measure median/p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT. We'll use wrk/locust + a small harness we provide.
[03:47] Dr. Sara Gomez: are you also going to gather percentiles like p95/p99 and histograms? We need raw traces.
[03:52] Liam Chen: yes we'll export raw logs and percentile buckets, plus profiles showing GPU utilization, token throughput, and latency breakdown (kernel time, compilation overhead, networking).
[04:03] Aaron Lee: how do we measure TTFT exactly in the pipeline? Frontend time vs Redwood time?
[04:08] Maya Patel: good point — we define two bounds: 1) agent-side TTFT (end-to-end from our frontend to first token delivered to user), and 2) platform TTFT (time from Redwood API receive to first token out). For the POC we'll capture both — Redwood will provide platform-side timings and you can correlate with your frontend metrics.
[04:28] Priya Nair: any thoughts on p95 vs p99 SLOs and error budgets? We're sensitive to p99.
[04:33] Liam Chen: recommend SLO set: TTFT p95 <= 150ms, TTFT p99 <= 300ms, TPOT p95 <= 15ms, TPOT p99 <= 30ms. Error budget we can set to 0.5% monthly for p99 violations during pilot. If that smells high we can adjust.
[04:50] Dr. Sara Gomez: could you run a baseline with Redwood Hosted and Dedicated equivalent? We want to see the delta.
[04:57] Maya Patel: yes we can run two configs: Redwood Hosted (our hosted API) and Redwood Dedicated (dedicated capacity). We'll flag expected differences: Hosted may have slightly higher TTFT variance due to multi-tenant scheduler and routing, Dedicated gives more predictable tail latencies.
[05:12] Aaron Lee: curious about our model — we'll use open-source Llama2-13B-8k quantized in FP16 as starting point, and maybe later try a 70B.
[05:20] Liam Chen: good call — starting with 13B is faster for iteration. For 70B we'll update targets: TPOT increases, so SLOs relaxed accordingly; we'll document that.
[05:28] Priya Nair: any tooling you provide for the measurement harness?
[05:31] Liam Chen: yes we'll give a repo with scripts to replay traces, run wrk/locust scenarios, and a runbook for measuring TTFT/TPOT. We also provide a dashboard template with p50/p95/p99 and histograms.
[05:45] Dr. Sara Gomez: will you instrument KV cache warmup? We want stable warm vs cold numbers.
[05:51] Liam Chen: yes test plan includes a warm phase of 10 minutes with representative queries, then the measurement window. For cold starts we restart the pool and measure first N requests.
[06:01] Maya Patel: timeline: we propose a 2-week pilot. Week 1: baseline runs (hosted + dedicated config), week 2: tuning (batching, quant, route policies) and final report. Deliverables: benchmark data, dashboard, and recommendation and pilot acceptance decision.
[06:16] Aaron Lee: that timeline works. can you send pricing/commit estimates for dedicated capacity if we want to run longer?
[06:23] Maya Patel: yes I'll include pricing options and rough cost estimate for the pilot and a monthly run rate for Dedicated.
[06:28] Priya Nair: success criteria — what concretely makes the POC a success for us?
[06:33] Dr. Sara Gomez: success = platform TTFT p95 <= 150ms and TPOT p95 <= 15ms under our steady 40 rps workload with KV warm, and we have docs to reproduce results. If Dedicated check passes, we consider expansion.
[06:47] Liam Chen: we'll also include a recommendation matrix: if we miss p95 by X% but meet p99, or vice versa, we give mitigations (more GPUs, different quant profile, or routing to lower latency region).
[06:58] Aaron Lee: any compliance concerns? We have PHI in some payloads; will private deployment be required?
[07:04] Maya Patel: we discussed Private options earlier — for this POC we can anonymize payloads and run on Hosted/Dedicated. If you need PHI in production we can run Private or VPC options; we'll include security docs.
[07:16] Priya Nair: jotting down next steps.
[07:20] Maya Patel: recap of next steps: we'll send the benchmark plan and scripts, you provide production traces and a prioritized prompt set, we'll schedule the first benchmark next Tuesday.
[07:31] Dr. Sara Gomez: I'll get the trace and prioritized prompt set to you by Friday.
[07:36] Maya Patel: perfect. anything else?
[07:38] Aaron Lee: not from me. thanks.
[07:40] Maya Patel: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the runbook and pricing.
[07:45] [meeting ends]
